hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties face millions in losses from property tax referendum
hero.teaser: Counties across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills, with potential losses in the tens of millions of dollars.
hero.body:
A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties offered estimates of the potential losses. Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County faces $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County faces $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said county officials are working with the Office of Management and Budget to determine the full impact. Powell said if there is a cut in property taxes, there will be real shortfalls and challenges, and revenue will have to be made up somewhere.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is more of a break for the struggling family in a $300,000 home working several jobs to make ends meet. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial race, warns against political demonization
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that when people constantly demonize someone to the point of suggesting they will destroy Florida, they give an opening to those with real mental health issues to commit violence. Though Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to harm others. The incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to become the state's next governor and succeed Ron DeSantis. "That's just reprehensible to me," he said of the threats.

cards.headline: Martin County battles 120-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue is battling a 120-acre brush fire in Indiantown.
cards.body: The blaze comes just days after Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a nearly 40-acre brush fire in the same area on Saturday.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing five foster children
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces charges after authorities discovered alleged abuse of five foster children living in her home.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce Pastor Arrested on Child Abuse Charges

A Fort Pierce pastor was arrested following an investigation into allegations of abuse involving five foster children in her care. Law enforcement discovered disturbing conditions at the pastor's home during their investigation, leading to formal charges against her.

The investigation revealed multiple serious allegations within the household. Police uncovered evidence of child abuse, along with conditions of severe neglect including starvation and filthy living environments. These findings prompted authorities to take immediate action to protect the children from further harm.

The case centers on five foster children who were residing with the pastor at the time of the discovery. All of the children were under her direct care and supervision as their foster parent. The conditions authorities found during their investigation were significant enough to warrant arrest and ongoing legal proceedings.

Authorities continue to investigate the full scope of what occurred in the home. The case remains active as law enforcement works to gather additional evidence and details about the abuse allegations. The foster children have been removed from the home and placed in protective custody.

cards.headline: 18-year-old charged with shooting 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old man was arrested in Fort Pierce after allegedly shooting a 17-year-old girl.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old man faces charges after allegedly shooting a 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce. The shooting occurred Saturday in the city.

Authorities arrested the suspect following the incident. The victim, a 17-year-old girl, was shot during the altercation.

Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The case remains under investigation by Fort Pierce authorities.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island could split in half as erosion threatens to breach Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A state report warns that nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with ocean water threatening to break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in two.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. According to the report, a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater, putting at risk the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in all of those areas.

Jupiter Island continues fighting erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. He added that if funding for beach renourishment goes away, "the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with."

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks as drought hits Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: State leaders are weighing a statewide fireworks ban for the Fourth of July as Florida faces drought conditions more severe than 1998, the last time such a ban was imposed.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders monitor severe drought conditions to determine whether a statewide fireworks ban is necessary. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban, cautioning that if drought conditions persist through the Fourth of July, a ban could be necessary. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said in May. Simpson acknowledged the significance of the nation's 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Murphy said the store monitors the drought index closely but remains optimistic about rainfall forecasts. The Department of Agriculture characterized a fireworks ban as a last resort.

hero.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
hero.teaser: ChildNet held its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
hero.body:
Thirty-five students reached a significant milestone by graduating at ChildNet's annual celebration held at Palm Beach State College. The event recognized the achievements of foster youth and young adults supported by the nonprofit organization, which operates in both Broward and Palm Beach counties. ChildNet provides comprehensive services to foster children and young adults, including educational support, adoption services, and resources for independent living.

Two graduates who stood out at the ceremony were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort. Both had experienced the loss of a parent and sought support from ChildNet during their high school years. The organization provided them with the resources and guidance they needed to overcome their challenges and move toward their futures. During the celebration, both graduates shared their experiences and offered encouragement to other young people facing similar hardships.

Diaz spoke directly to others in comparable situations, emphasizing the importance of maintaining hope and persistence. She encouraged her peers to believe in their potential for success, invest effort into their education, and never abandon their goals despite difficulties. She stressed the value of pushing through pain and continuing to work hard toward one's objectives. Saintfort delivered a similar message, highlighting the power of believing in oneself as a foundation for achievement. Both young adults demonstrated a commitment to motivating others who might be struggling with loss and uncertainty.

Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, used the occasion to acknowledge the collective effort behind the graduates' success. He recognized the contributions of case workers employed by ChildNet and the Department of Children and Families, as well as the dedication of the students themselves. Rein emphasized that the evening represented the culmination of hard work from everyone involved in supporting these young people. Looking ahead, Diaz has enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with aspirations to become a doctor. Saintfort is pursuing a vocational program to train as a plumber. Both are positioning themselves for stable, rewarding careers after graduation.

cards.headline: Florida voters split on property tax proposal ahead of November ballot
cards.teaser: A ballot measure that would raise the homestead exemption and roll back property taxes is drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The measure needs 60% approval to pass.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Reactions from West Palm Beach residents are mixed. Brian Edington supports the proposal because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida as homeowners. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood as an example, noting that trash services are picked up twice weekly when once a week would be adequate. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding, saying "There's going to be less money ... because everything is expensive now." While homeowners were generally supportive, renters expressed skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach them, stating "Pretty sure they're going to raise the rent on everybody, all the renters."

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance swamped as 8,000 calls come in monthly
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple hours each month, far outpacing the nearly $2 million in grant funding available.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. Yet demand vastly outweighs available resources. Program director Dr. James Green told WPTV that the county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly, combined with data from 211. Currently, about 800 applications are in the queue for rental assistance. Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill rapidly, with the program typically receiving about 600 applications within the first couple of hours. At the time of this report, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa and spent 12 years as an educator before switching to real estate, described the strain: "Almost every day, all the bills are rising except our paychecks." Green said preventing homelessness depends on community involvement and is calling on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need. For those unable to access the county program, 211 offers another resource available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban off state coast
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding in waters within 200 miles of Florida has cleared the U.S. House, drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry.
cards.body:
The measure, H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, Florida's shark diving industry opposes the bill, arguing it unfairly targets conservation-driven tourism businesses while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators avoid surface chumming and instead take bait underwater during dives, a practice they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food. "What we're really requesting is the chance to speak and share the science and the facts," Campbell said. "No one from Congress has yet asked us to present data or explain our practices."

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, contend the Hawaii experience demonstrates different results. Ajemian says shark diving in Florida has a "near perfect safety record" for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: Indian River, Martin and St.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen. The ban is designed to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms in local waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said composting provides a good alternative during the ban period. According to Ricketts, a small trash can is sufficient for most home composting needs and is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscaping and gardens.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
cards.teaser: Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will be prohibited from using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns and landscaping during the rainy season.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup, Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs after eating them and is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart for $50,000 in damages.
cards.body:
An Okeechobee County woman is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after claiming she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs and subsequently developed parasitic infections and other medical complications. Mary Hubbard purchased the product in June 2024 at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the complaint, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food and documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product.

The lawsuit alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. Hubbard is seeking $50,000 in damages. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart stated it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance overwhelmed by demand as Treasure Coast families struggle
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but has only $2 million in combined grant funding to meet the demand.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program is being overwhelmed by demand from residents struggling with rising housing costs. The Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding available, but the need far exceeds available resources. Dr. James Green, the program's director, told WPTV that the county typically receives about 600 applications within the first couple of hours each month. Currently, approximately 800 applications are queued for assistance. "We're doing what we can to prioritize and serve those who are most needy but the demand far outweighs the resources that are available," Green said. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month.

Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Dr. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. The surge in applications stems partly from rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food. Green noted that there are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month combined with 211. For those unable to access the county program, Green recommends calling 211, available 24/7, which connects residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs. Green is also calling on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.body:
Demolition crews began this week dismantling portions of the Indian River Mall in Vero Beach to make way for a revitalization project. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said crews are working on the first phase, taking down the Macy's location and the structure where Sears once operated. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition work. Mary Alice Stopyra expressed her approval, saying the building "degraded over time." Mark Manera, a long-time mall visitor, described it as "the death of a beautiful building" and noted a "steady decline year after year after year." Despite his sadness about the structure's demise, Manera said the community needs this change and that new jobs and opportunities would be wonderful.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He characterized the new development as "a city within a city," contrasting it with the deteriorated mall of recent years. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, while the team continues working on permitting for the remaining phases of the project.

hero.headline: 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Atlantic Ocean to Lake Worth Beach for Cystic Fibrosis
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean to arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling.
hero.body:
The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis brings more than 100 paddlers across 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis. Participants launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, established by event founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

All paddlers must wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, and crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum with final contributions due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration marking the paddlers' arrival.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Closes Sunday at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
cards.body:
"Beetlejuice" the musical has landed at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon in the iconic striped suit from Tim Burton's 1988 film. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger said. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with audiences. "I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them. That's my favorite part of theater," he explained. Early in the run, an unexpected moment occurred during an onstage wig change when the second wig came off with the first, leaving him bald for an entire scene. Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker launches Congressional campaign in CD 11
hero.teaser: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Representative Daniel Webster, setting up a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini.
hero.body:
Carey Baker, the former Lake County Property Appraiser, has entered the race for Florida's 11th Congressional District seat. The 63-year-old Republican is competing in a primary field that includes Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, described as one of Baker's former protégés who has previously run for the seat. Baker has deep roots in the district and a lengthy record of public service spanning more than two decades.

Baker has represented much of Central Florida in the state legislature, serving in both the Florida House and Senate before being elected as the county's Property Appraiser. A lifelong Eustis resident, he has maintained prominence in Republican politics since his initial election to the Florida House in 2000. His family has a history of legislative service, with his father also having represented the area in the state House. After losing his bid for re-election as Property Appraiser in 2024, Baker pursued another leadership position within the local party structure, working alongside Sabatini in a campaign to become Lake County Republican Party Chair, though that effort proved unsuccessful.

In his 2024 Property Appraiser race, Baker ran as a write-in candidate but was defeated decisively. Republican David Jordan, who filed as an official candidate, defeated Baker by a margin of three to one in the General Election. Despite this loss, Baker demonstrated strong fundraising abilities that will serve him in the primary race. He raised $233,000 for his Property Appraiser campaign and has already begun building financial support for his Congressional bid. Florida's 11th Congressional District encompasses all of Sumter County, portions of western Orange County, and the majority of Lake County.

The district leans heavily Republican, with more than 57 percent of voters supporting President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, making a GOP nominee likely to prevail in November. On the Democratic side, repeat candidate Barbie Harden Hall suspended her campaign on Saturday due to health issues. Hall had been the leading fundraiser among Democratic candidates and appeared to be the party's strongest choice for the nomination. Three other Democratic candidates remain in the race: Royal Webster, Shawn Bettis, and Dan Williams.

cards.headline: Tampa City Council Chair seeks delay on Rays stadium CRA vote amid ongoing negotiations
cards.teaser: Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin is pushing to delay a Community Redevelopment Agency discussion tied to the Tampa Bay Rays stadium proposal, saying the issue is not ready for a vote as negotiations continue.
cards.body:
Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin submitted a memo last week requesting that the Rays stadium item be deferred from next week's Tampa CRA meeting until at least July, and possibly longer. Clendenin told Florida Politics that negotiations remain ongoing and that discussing the matter prematurely would be inappropriate. "There's a lot of things happening behind the scenes. There's a lot of negotiations happening, and of course with the chaos happening in Tallahassee, until we can all kind of see everything out front, it's just premature on Thursday to bring it to the table," Clendenin said. He disputed Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal's characterization of the negotiations' status and cited recent uncertainty over property tax reform as an additional factor for negotiators to consider.

The Rays stadium MOU approved by Tampa and Hillsborough County includes $80 million from the city of Tampa and $100 million tied to the Tampa CRA, along with other public dollars. Clendenin emphasized that the financing structure remains under active negotiation and that earlier votes by the City Council and County Commission represented support for the general direction of the non-binding MOU, not final approval of CRA terms. Several options remain on the table for the CRA-related portion, including not using the CRA, creating a different type of district, or using another special district structure. "For the CRA portion, nothing has been agreed to by any party," Clendenin said.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial race, warns against political demonization
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that when people constantly demonize someone to the point of suggesting they will destroy Florida, they give an opening to those with real mental health issues to commit violence. Though Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to harm others. The incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to become the state's next governor and succeed Ron DeSantis. "That's just reprehensible to me," he said of the threats.

cards.headline: Cuba's former President Raúl Castro makes first public appearance since U.S. indictment
cards.teaser: Raúl Castro, Cuba's low-profile former president, appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft.
cards.body:
Cuba's former President Raúl Castro made his first public appearance since a U.S. indictment when he celebrated his 95th birthday Friday night at the Ministry of Interior in Havana. State television broadcast footage showing Castro, dressed in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater to a standing ovation, accompanied by his grandson and bodyguard Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel. The celebration gave Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to project defiance as the Trump administration escalates pressure on the fuel-starved island.

Díaz-Canel delivered a tribute to Castro and his late brother Fidel, calling Raúl Castro a target for enemy intelligence services because of his "courage and loyalty." He repeated the slogan "Raúl is Raúl," echoing billboards across Havana and social media posts that appeared since the May 20 U.S. indictment on murder charges. The Justice Department accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of two civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. The indictment represents an escalation following the Trump administration's January move to cut off Cuba's oil supplies, worsening blackouts and a public health crisis. The administration demands Cuba release political prisoners, implement economic reforms and change its governance to avoid becoming a national security threat.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second campaign for Jacksonville House District 12
cards.teaser: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second campaign for Jacksonville House District 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The 22-year-old candidate filed for the race Friday, just three days before qualifying began Monday, June 8. Sandlin said the Florida Democratic Party agreed the seat was too close in the 2024 election to leave uncontested. "That'd be a huge missed opportunity to have an extra voice for labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature," Sandlin told Florida Politics on Saturday morning. The Republican-leaning seat is open because Duggan is term-limited.

Sandlin had previously filed for Jacksonville City Council District 7 to succeed Democrat Jimmy Peluso, who launched a run for an at-large seat. He dropped out of that race, which remains crowded with six Democrats and a no party affiliation candidate. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, Sandlin is likely to advance to the November ballot upon qualifying. Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is also running in HD 12. Through the end of May, Freeman raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee called For the Future We Want, with roughly $390,000 on hand.

cards.headline: Senator Rick Scott honors father's D-Day service, vows continued support for military and veterans
cards.teaser: Senator Rick Scott is remembering what many members of the military had to do on D-Day, the famous 1944 World War II military operation wherein more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy.
cards.body:
On Saturday, Senator Rick Scott, a Naples Republican and Navy veteran, honored the memory of D-Day and his adopted father, Orba Scott, who participated in the historic 1944 World War II operation. More than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy during D-Day, making first headway in the liberation of German-occupied France. According to Sen. Scott, his adopted father parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

"My father was blessed enough to return home from battle, but many brave individuals made the last full measure of devotion in defense of freedom and didn't return home," Sen. Scott said. The Senator vowed to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. "As a Senator, a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, I am fighting every day to improve our military, take care of our nation's veterans, and protect your legacy so the next generation knows and appreciate the sacrifices made for their freedoms," he said.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration in Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adul.
cards.body:
35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. ChildNet supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward. Diaz shared a message for others in similar situations, saying "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard." Saintfort echoed that sentiment, saying "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff." Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber. CEO Larry N. Rein reflected on the significance of the evening, saying "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!"

hero.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing five foster children
hero.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces charges after authorities discovered alleged abuse of five foster children living in her home.
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Pastor Arrested on Child Abuse Charges

A Fort Pierce pastor was arrested following an investigation into allegations of abuse involving five foster children in her care. Law enforcement discovered disturbing conditions at the pastor's home during their investigation, leading to formal charges against her.

The investigation revealed multiple serious allegations within the household. Police uncovered evidence of child abuse, along with conditions of severe neglect including starvation and filthy living environments. These findings prompted authorities to take immediate action to protect the children from further harm.

The case centers on five foster children who were residing with the pastor at the time of the discovery. All of the children were under her direct care and supervision as their foster parent. The conditions authorities found during their investigation were significant enough to warrant arrest and ongoing legal proceedings.

Authorities continue to investigate the full scope of what occurred in the home. The case remains active as law enforcement works to gather additional evidence and details about the abuse allegations. The foster children have been removed from the home and placed in protective custody.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: A ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen took effect June 1 in Indian River, Martin and St.
cards.body:
A ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen is now in effect in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. The restriction applies to lawns and landscaping throughout the three counties.

Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban aims to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. According to Skaggs, these blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an alternative during the ban. Ricketts said using a small trash can is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscapes during the fertilizer restriction period.

Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will ban any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen starting June 30. The ban applies to lawns and landscaping throughout the rainy season to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that can cause algae blooms in local waterways.

Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the blooms could disrupt the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. Algae can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said composting offers a good alternative during the ban. A small trash can provides the easiest and most practical way to compost for home landscapes and gardens to add nutrients without fertilizer.
